chunks.topic: Flip-Flops as the Basic Memory Element
chunks.summary: A general digital system combines combinational logic gates with memory devices; the flip-flop (FF) — also called a latch or bistable multivibrator — is the most important memory element, built from an assembly of logic gates.
chunks.text: A general digital system is organized as combinational logic (gates that compute outputs purely from present inputs) combined with memory devices that retain state across time. The most important memory element used for this purpose is the flip-flop (FF), which is itself built from an interconnected assembly of ordinary logic gates (typically NAND or NOR gates) wired with feedback. The flip-flop is known by several other names depending on context: latch and bistable multivibrator both refer to the same fundamental idea — a circuit with two stable output states that will hold (remember) whichever state it was last set to, until deliberately changed.
chunks.figure_note: Page 3 shows a block diagram of a general digital system combining a combinational-logic block with a memory (flip-flop) block, with feedback from the memory outputs back into the combinational logic — this is the canonical sequential-circuit model (Moore/Mealy style). Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering is unavailable here.

chunks.topic: NAND Gate Latch (Basic SET/RESET Latch)
chunks.summary: Two cross-coupled NAND gates form the basic SET-RESET latch with active-LOW inputs: pulsing SET LOW forces Q=1 (Q'=0), pulsing RESET (CLEAR) LOW forces Q=0 (Q'=1), and both inputs HIGH is the normal resting/hold state.
chunks.text:
The NAND gate latch (simply called 'the latch') is the most basic flip-flop, built from two NAND gates cross-coupled so each gate's output feeds back as one input to the other gate. Its two inputs are SET and RESET (also called CLEAR), and — because they are built from NAND gates — both inputs are ACTIVE-LOW: the output only changes in response to a LOW pulse on an input, not a HIGH one. When the latch is SET, Q=1 and Q'=0. When the latch is CLEAR/RESET, Q=0 and Q'=1.

Setting the latch: pulsing the SET input LOW (momentarily) drives Q HIGH regardless of whether Q was already 0 or already 1 beforehand — in both starting cases Q ends up HIGH after the SET pulse, and stays HIGH after SET returns to its inactive (HIGH) level.

Resetting the latch: pulsing RESET LOW (momentarily) drives Q LOW regardless of whether Q was 0 or 1 beforehand — in both cases Q ends up LOW after the pulse and stays LOW after RESET returns HIGH.

Summary of all four input combinations for the active-LOW NAND latch (inputs written as SET, RESET; 0 = active/LOW, 1 = inactive/HIGH): 
- SET=1, RESET=1 (both inactive): normal resting/hold state — Q and Q' remain in whatever state they were in previously (memory behavior). 
- SET=0, RESET=1: latch is SET — Q goes to (and stays at) 1, even after SET returns HIGH. 
- SET=1, RESET=0: latch is CLEARED/RESET — Q goes to (and stays at) 0, even after RESET returns HIGH. 
- SET=0, RESET=0: an INVALID/forbidden condition — the latch tries to set and clear simultaneously, forcing Q = Q' = 1, which violates the normal Q'=NOT(Q) relationship; the resulting state when both inputs return HIGH together is unpredictable (a race condition), so this input combination should never be used deliberately.
chunks.figure_note: Page 8 shows alternate equivalent representations of the NAND latch (the two cross-coupled NAND gates alongside a simplified block/box symbol with SET, RESET inputs and Q, Q' outputs). Pages 6-7 show the two 'starting from Q=0' vs 'starting from Q=1' timing cases for SET and RESET pulses. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here; the logical behavior above is standard NAND-latch theory and internally consistent.

chunks.topic: NOR Gate Latch
chunks.summary: Two cross-coupled NOR gates form a latch functionally similar to the NAND latch but with active-HIGH SET/RESET inputs (and Q, Q' outputs swapped in position relative to the NAND version); the forbidden state is SET=1,RESET=1 giving Q=Q'=0.
chunks.text:
A NOR-gate latch is built the same way as the NAND latch but with two cross-coupled NOR gates instead, which inverts the active level of the control inputs: SET and RESET are ACTIVE-HIGH for the NOR latch (the output changes when an input is pulsed HIGH, not LOW). Functionally it behaves like the NAND latch, but the Q and Q' output positions are reversed relative to the NAND-latch circuit, and the whole truth table is 'inverted' in terms of which level is active.

Summary of the NOR latch (inputs SET, RESET; 1 = active/HIGH here): 
- SET=0, RESET=0 (both inactive): normal resting/hold state — no effect on the output, whatever state Q was in is retained. 
- SET=1, RESET=0: latch is SET — Q always goes to (and remains at) 1, even after SET returns to 0. 
- SET=0, RESET=1: latch is CLEARED — Q always goes to (and remains at) 0, even after RESET returns to 0. 
- SET=1, RESET=1: INVALID/forbidden condition — tries to set and reset simultaneously, forcing Q = Q' = 0 (note: 0, not 1 as in the NAND-latch invalid case), and produces an unpredictable result when both inputs return to 0 together; this combination should not be used.

When power is first applied to any latch/FF, its starting output state cannot be predicted if both SET and RESET are left in their inactive state — to guarantee a known starting state, the latch must be deliberately placed into that state by momentarily activating SET or RESET once, typically via an initialization/power-on-reset pulse.
chunks.figure_note: Page 10 shows the two cross-coupled NOR gates forming the latch, with SET and RESET labeled as active-HIGH inputs. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here; the truth table above follows directly from NOR-gate logic and is internally consistent (dual of the NAND latch).

chunks.topic: Troubleshooting Case Study: Latch Circuit
chunks.summary: A worked troubleshooting example for a NAND-latch circuit where Q appears stuck LOW: possible causes include an open connection preventing Q from responding, an internal NAND-gate failure, or an internal/external short of the relevant pin to ground.
chunks.text: This is a worked troubleshooting case study on a NAND-latch (labeled Z1/Z2 gates) circuit. If Q output is found stuck LOW (not responding to SET pulses as expected), several distinct fault hypotheses must be considered and each checked/eliminated systematically: (1) an internal open connection at a specific gate pin (e.g. Z1 pin 1) that prevents Q from responding to the input signal at all; (2) an internal component failure inside NAND gate Z1 that prevents it from switching properly even though its pins are electrically intact; (3) the Q output node itself stuck LOW, which could be caused by any of several distinct short-to-ground faults: gate Z1's pin 3 or pin 4 internally shorted to ground, gate Z2's pin 2 internally shorted to ground, or the Q net externally shorted to ground somewhere on the board. The teaching point is that a single observed symptom ('Q stuck LOW') can have multiple distinct root causes at different points in the circuit, so troubleshooting must isolate which one it actually is (e.g. via voltage/resistance measurements or by lifting/isolating pins) rather than guessing.
chunks.figure_note: Page 13 shows the specific NAND-latch schematic (gates labeled Z1, Z2 with pin numbers) used for this troubleshooting exercise. Exact pin/wire layout not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here; the fault list above is transcribed directly from the slide text.

chunks.topic: Digital Pulses: Rise Time, Fall Time, Pulse Width
chunks.summary: A pulse waveform switches between an active and inactive level (positive pulses are active-HIGH, negative pulses are active-LOW); real transitions take finite time, characterized by rise time tr (10%-90% on the leading edge), fall time tf (90%-10% on the trailing edge), and pulse width tw (measured at the 50% points).
chunks.text:
A pulse waveform is a signal that switches between an active state and an inactive state. A POSITIVE pulse has an active-HIGH level (it idles LOW and pulses HIGH). A NEGATIVE pulse has an active-LOW level (it idles HIGH and pulses LOW).

In real circuits, a signal cannot change instantaneously between levels — it takes finite time. Three standard timing parameters describe this: 
- Rise time (tr): the time for a LOW-to-HIGH transition (on a positive-going edge), measured between the points where the waveform crosses 10% and 90% of its full transition height on the leading edge. 
- Fall time (tf): the time for a HIGH-to-LOW transition, measured between the points where the waveform crosses 90% and 10% of its full transition height on the trailing edge. 
- Pulse width (tw): the duration of the pulse, measured as the time between the point where the leading edge crosses 50% of the HIGH level and the point where the trailing edge crosses 50% of the HIGH level.

These parameters matter because flip-flop and gate datasheets specify minimum pulse widths and maximum allowable rise/fall times for reliable clocking and triggering — a clock or trigger pulse that is too narrow, or whose edges are too slow, can cause a flip-flop to respond unreliably or not at all.
chunks.figure_note: Pages 15-16 show idealized positive-pulse and negative-pulse waveforms. Pages 17-19 show a real (non-ideal, sloped-edge) pulse waveform with tr, tf, and tw marked at the 10%/90%/50% crossing points respectively. Exact waveform drawing not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here; the definitions above are standard and match the slide captions.

chunks.topic: Clock Signals and Clocked Flip-Flops (edges, setup time, hold time)
chunks.summary: Synchronous systems change state only at a specific point in the clock cycle (a positive-going or negative-going transition), unlike asynchronous systems which respond immediately to any input change; clocked FFs require their synchronous control inputs to be stable for a setup time before, and a hold time after, the active clock edge.
chunks.text:
Digital systems operate either asynchronously (outputs can change state the instant any input changes, with no reference clock) or synchronously (outputs can only change state at a specific point in the clock cycle, regardless of when the data inputs actually changed). The clock signal itself is a rectangular pulse train or square wave. A Positive-Going Transition (PGT) is when the clock goes from 0 to 1; a Negative-Going Transition (NGT) is when the clock goes from 1 to 0 — these transitions are also generically called edges.

Clocked flip-flops change their output state only on one particular clock edge (either PGT or NGT, depending on the specific FF's design), and their clock input is typically labeled CLK, CK, or CP. On a logic symbol, a small triangle at the CLK input pin indicates the FF is edge-triggered on the PGT; a bubble combined with a triangle indicates NGT triggering.

Data/control inputs on a clocked FF (like S, R, J, K, D) only affect the output at the active clock transition, which is why they are called synchronous control inputs — changing them at other times merely 'gets the FF ready' to change, but the actual output change is held off (triggered) until the next active CLK edge arrives.

Two critical timing requirements govern reliable synchronous operation: Setup time (tS) is the minimum interval BEFORE the active clock transition during which the synchronous control input(s) must already be held at their correct, stable level. Hold time (tH) is the minimum interval AFTER the active clock transition during which the synchronous control input(s) must continue to be held stable. Violating either requirement (changing the data input too close to the clock edge) can cause the FF to enter an unpredictable or metastable output state.
chunks.figure_note: Page 22 shows FF logic-symbol clock-input variants: plain triangle (PGT-triggered) vs bubble+triangle (NGT-triggered). Pages 24-25 show waveform diagrams marking the setup-time window before, and hold-time window after, the active clock edge relative to a control-input transition. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here; the definitions above match standard FF timing theory and the slide captions.

chunks.topic: Clocked (Edge-Triggered) S-R Flip-Flop
chunks.summary: The clocked S-R FF behaves like the S-R latch but only responds to its S and R inputs at the active clock edge (PGT or NGT depending on design); internally it is built from a basic NAND latch, a pulse-steering circuit, and an edge-detector network.
chunks.text:
The clocked (edge-triggered) S-R flip-flop adds a CLK trigger input to the basic S-R latch behavior: the S and R inputs are synchronous control inputs that determine what state the FF WILL go to, but the actual state change only happens at the occurrence of the active clock edge (either a PGT- or NGT-triggered version exists — both are used in practice). Before that active edge occurs, changing S or R has no effect on the output; the FF 'remembers' the S/R condition present just prior to the edge and applies it exactly at the edge.

A PGT-triggered S-R FF: S and R control the resulting state the same way as described for the basic NOR-gate latch (S sets Q=1, R resets Q=0, S=R=inactive holds state, S=R=active is invalid), but the change is deferred until the next positive-going clock edge. A corresponding NGT-triggered S-R FF behaves identically except it responds on the negative-going edge instead.

Internally, an edge-triggered S-R FF is built from three sections: (1) a basic NAND-gate latch (the two output-holding NAND gates, often labeled NAND-3 and NAND-4) that stores the actual Q/Q' state; (2) a pulse-steering circuit (typically two more NAND gates, NAND-1 and NAND-2) that routes the S and R signals toward the latch only when enabled by the edge detector; (3) an edge-detector circuit that generates a very brief internal pulse (typically 2-5 ns wide) exactly at the moment of the desired clock transition (PGT or NGT), momentarily enabling the steering gates so the latch captures S/R only during that narrow window — this is what makes the overall device 'edge-triggered' rather than level-triggered like a plain latch.
chunks.figure_note: Page 27 shows the PGT-triggered S-R FF symbol/circuit; page 28 shows its input/output waveform timing diagram; page 29 shows the NGT-triggered version. Page 30 shows the internal block structure (NAND latch + steering NANDs + edge detector). Page 31 shows two small edge-detector implementations, (a) for PGT and (b) for NGT, each producing a narrow ~2-5 ns internal pulse. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here; descriptions summarized from slide captions.

chunks.topic: Clocked J-K Flip-Flop
chunks.summary: The J-K flip-flop behaves like the S-R FF (J=SET, K=CLEAR) but eliminates the invalid input combination: when J=K=1, the output toggles to its opposite state at the active clock edge, making it more versatile than the S-R FF.
chunks.text:
The clocked J-K flip-flop operates like the clocked S-R flip-flop, with J playing the role of SET and K playing the role of CLEAR/RESET. The key improvement over the S-R FF is that the previously-forbidden 'both active' input combination is redefined into a useful TOGGLE mode: when J and K are both HIGH at the active clock edge, the output flips to the opposite of its previous state (Q becomes Q', and vice versa) rather than producing an invalid/unpredictable result. Like the S-R FF, a J-K FF can be built to trigger on either the positive-going or the negative-going clock edge.

Because it has no ambiguous/forbidden state, the J-K FF is considered much more versatile than the S-R FF: it can do everything the S-R FF does (J=1,K=0 sets; J=0,K=1 resets; J=K=0 holds) PLUS it adds the toggle capability (J=K=1), which is essential for building binary counters (each J-K FF configured in toggle mode divides its clock frequency by 2).

Internally, the edge-triggered J-K FF contains the same three functional sections as the edge-triggered S-R FF (a NAND output latch, pulse-steering NAND gates, and an edge-detector circuit), with additional feedback from the Q/Q' outputs back into the steering gates so that the toggle behavior can be realized (the current output state gates which of J or K is allowed to affect the next state).
chunks.figure_note: Page 33 shows the PGT-triggered J-K FF symbol; page 34 shows the NGT-triggered version. Page 35 shows the internal gate-level circuitry (NAND latch + steering gates + edge detector, with output feedback enabling toggle mode). Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Clocked D Flip-Flop and Parallel Data Transfer
chunks.summary: The D flip-flop has a single data input D; at the active clock edge, Q simply takes on whatever value D had, making it ideal for storing/transferring a single bit. A D FF can be built from a J-K FF by tying K to the inverted J (D) input. Multiple D FFs sharing a common clock implement parallel data transfer.
chunks.text:
The clocked D (Data) flip-flop has only one data input, D. At the active clock edge (positive-going or negative-going, depending on the specific device), the output Q is set to whatever logic value is present on D at that instant — Q simply 'follows' D, sampled once per active clock edge. This single-input behavior makes the D FF especially useful for storing and transferring binary data one bit at a time.

A D flip-flop can be implemented directly from a J-K flip-flop by tying the K input to the J input through an inverter (so K is always the complement of J=D): when D=1, J=1 and K=0, which sets Q=1; when D=0, J=0 and K=1, which resets Q=0 — exactly reproducing D-FF behavior. The same inverter trick (tying R to the complement of S) converts an S-R FF into a D FF as well.

Parallel data transfer example: three signal lines X, Y, Z need to be captured into three storage FFs Q1, Q2, Q3. Using three D flip-flops (one per bit, D input tied to X/Y/Z respectively) with their CLK inputs tied together to a common TRANSFER pulse line, all three levels present on X, Y, Z at the moment of the TRANSFER pulse's active edge get captured into Q1, Q2, Q3 simultaneously. This is the defining characteristic of parallel data transfer: multiple bits move from source to destination(s) at the same instant, using one shared clock/transfer pulse, rather than moving one bit at a time.
chunks.figure_note: Page 37 shows the PGT-triggered D FF symbol. Page 38 shows a J-K FF with an added inverter (K tied to NOT(J)=NOT(D)) implementing D-FF behavior. Pages 39-40 show three D flip-flops with inputs X, Y, Z and a shared CLK/TRANSFER line feeding outputs Q1, Q2, Q3, illustrating parallel transfer. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: D Latch (Transparent Latch)
chunks.summary: Removing the edge-detector circuit from an edge-triggered D flip-flop turns it into a D latch (transparent latch): the output follows the D input continuously whenever the control input (called EN, not CLK) is at its active level, rather than only at a clock edge.
chunks.text:
The edge-triggered D flip-flop relies on an internal edge-detector circuit to ensure Q only responds to D at the instant of the active clock transition. If that edge-detector circuit is omitted, the resulting circuit is instead a D LATCH (also called a transparent latch): while the control input is at its active level, Q continuously follows (is 'transparent' to) whatever value is present on D — it is level-sensitive rather than edge-sensitive, and Q can change multiple times during one active period if D changes multiple times.

Structurally, the D latch circuit still contains the NAND output latch plus the two steering NAND gates (gates 1 and 2) from the edge-triggered design, but WITHOUT the edge-detector network. Because there's no edge detector, the effect on Q and Q' is not restricted to only happen at a transition — hence the common control input is called an ENABLE input (abbreviated EN) rather than a CLK (clock) input, to emphasize that it behaves as a level-sensitive gate/window rather than an edge trigger.
chunks.figure_note: Page 42 shows the D-latch internal structure, its function table (Q follows D while EN is active; holds when EN inactive), and its logic symbol (EN input, no clock-triangle marking). Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Asynchronous Inputs (PRESET / CLEAR)
chunks.summary: Most clocked FFs also have asynchronous PRESET (PRE) and CLEAR (CLR) inputs that force Q to a known state immediately, independent of the clock; these are typically active-LOW and are tied to their inactive level when not used, and are clearly distinguished from the synchronous SET/RESET control inputs.
chunks.text:
Inputs whose effect depends on the clock edge are called synchronous inputs (e.g. S, R, J, K, D as discussed in earlier sections). Most clocked flip-flops ALSO provide asynchronous inputs that act immediately, completely independent of the clock — these are conventionally labeled PRE (PRESET, forces Q=1) and CLR (CLEAR, forces Q=0). Asynchronous inputs are commonly active-LOW, shown with an overbar on the label (PRE-bar, CLR-bar) and an inversion bubble on the FF symbol; when not used, they must be tied to their inactive level (HIGH, for active-LOW versions) so they don't unintentionally override the clocked behavior.

Because IC manufacturers historically did not standardize this nomenclature, other labels for the same asynchronous functions appear in datasheets, including S-D (direct SET) and R-D (direct RESET) — but regardless of the label used, these must be clearly distinguished from the synchronous SET/RESET (S/R) control inputs discussed earlier, since PRE/CLR bypass the clock entirely while S/R only take effect at an active clock edge. A typical example is a J-K flip-flop that triggers on the negative-going clock edge and additionally has active-LOW asynchronous PRE and CLR inputs for immediate, clock-independent forcing of the output (e.g. for system initialization/reset).
chunks.figure_note: Page 45 shows a clocked J-K FF symbol augmented with PRE and CLR inputs. Page 47 shows a NGT-triggered J-K FF with active-LOW PRE-bar/CLR-bar inputs (inversion bubbles shown on those pins). Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Flip-Flop Timing Considerations: Datasheet Parameters
chunks.summary: Key FF datasheet timing parameters include setup/hold time, propagation delay (tPLH/tPHL), maximum clocking frequency (fMAX), minimum clock HIGH/LOW pulse widths (tW(H)/tW(L)), minimum asynchronous active pulse width, and maximum clock transition time — all of which bound reliable operation.
chunks.text:
Important flip-flop timing parameters (found on manufacturer datasheets) include: Setup time and hold time (already covered in 5-5) — the windows around the active clock edge during which synchronous inputs must be stable. Propagation delay (tPLH for LOW-to-HIGH output transitions, tPHL for HIGH-to-LOW) — the time from the triggering clock edge until the output actually settles to its new value; these are typically specified as MAXIMUM values (the worst case the device is guaranteed not to exceed). Maximum clocking frequency (fMAX) — the highest clock frequency at which the FF is guaranteed to still respond reliably. Clock pulse HIGH and LOW times (tW(H), tW(L)) — the minimum time the clock must remain HIGH, and the minimum time it must remain LOW, between transitions, for reliable triggering; these are specified as MINIMUM values. Asynchronous active pulse width — the minimum time an asynchronous input (PRE/CLR) must be held HIGH before going LOW (and LOW before going HIGH) to reliably force its effect; also a minimum value. Clock transition time — the maximum allowable rise/fall time of the clock edge itself for the FF to trigger reliably (typically under about 50 ns for TTL devices and under about 200 ns for CMOS devices — CMOS tolerates slower edges than TTL).

Manufacturer datasheets tabulate these values for specific FF part numbers; the general rule is that ALL of these listed parameters are MINIMUM required values EXCEPT propagation delay figures, which are MAXIMUM values (i.e., you must meet-or-exceed the minimums, and the device won't exceed the stated maximum delay).
chunks.figure_note: Page 49 shows a waveform diagram marking tPLH/tPHL propagation delays and the clock's tW(H)/tW(L)/asynchronous pulse-width windows. Page 50 shows a tabulated set of real manufacturer timing values for one or more specific FF part numbers. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Potential Timing Problems Between Cascaded Flip-Flops
chunks.summary: When one FF's output feeds directly into another FF's synchronous input and both share the same clock edge, propagation delay could in principle cause unreliable operation, but because edge-triggered FFs typically have very short (often zero) hold-time requirements, the driven FF reliably captures the driving FF's PRE-transition value.
chunks.text:
A potential timing hazard arises whenever the output of one flip-flop connects to the synchronous (data) input of a second flip-flop, and both FFs are triggered by the identical clock signal and edge. Naively, one might worry that the first FF's output changes (after its propagation delay) right around the same clock edge that is also supposed to load that changing value into the second FF, causing unpredictable results.

In practice, this is not usually a problem because edge-triggered FFs have very short hold-time requirements — 5 ns or less, and many real FFs have tH = 0 (no hold-time requirement at all). Given that the driven FF's hold time is short enough, a reliable general rule applies: a flip-flop's output goes to the state determined by the logic levels present at its synchronous control inputs JUST PRIOR TO the active clock transition — i.e., the driven FF effectively 'sees' and captures the driving FF's OLD (pre-edge) output value, not its new one, because the driving FF's output hasn't had time to actually change yet at the instant the shared edge occurs (thanks to the driving FF's own nonzero propagation delay). Concretely: Q2 (second FF) will respond correctly to the value present at Q1 prior to the negative-going clock transition, provided Q2's hold-time requirement (tH) is shorter than Q1's propagation delay (tPHL/tPLH) — which is true for essentially all real edge-triggered FF families, making this a safe, standard cascading pattern (e.g. used throughout shift registers and ripple/synchronous counters).
chunks.figure_note: Page 52 shows two cascaded FFs (Q1 feeding Q2's data input, shared NGT clock) with a timing diagram illustrating that Q2 samples Q1's pre-edge value because tH(Q2) < tPHL(Q1). Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Flip-Flop Applications and Synchronizing Asynchronous Inputs
chunks.summary: FFs are used for counting, storing binary data, and transferring binary data — categorized as sequential applications where outputs follow a predetermined state sequence. Because most systems are synchronous while real-world (human) inputs are asynchronous, an edge-triggered D FF is commonly used to 'synchronize' an asynchronous signal to the system clock before it gates other logic, avoiding unpredictable partial pulses.
chunks.text:
Common flip-flop applications include: counting (each FF divides/counts clock transitions), storing binary data (a group of FFs forms a register), and transferring binary data between locations. Many of these are classified as sequential applications, meaning the output follows a predetermined sequence of states over time (as opposed to combinational logic, whose output depends only on the present inputs).

Most digital systems operate primarily synchronously (state changes are gated by a system clock), but asynchronous inputs (most commonly from human interaction — a switch or button press) are unavoidable and get combined with synchronous logic. The problem: an asynchronous signal can change at any random instant relative to a clock or gating signal, so directly gating a signal with a raw asynchronous input (e.g. ANDing it with a clock) can produce unpredictable PARTIAL pulses at the output — a spurious short pulse rather than a clean full pulse, which downstream logic may misinterpret. The fix is to first pass the asynchronous signal through an edge-triggered D flip-flop clocked by the system clock: this 'synchronizes' the signal so that it changes only in step with (immediately after) a clock edge, producing a clean, full-width output that can then safely enable/gate other synchronous logic (e.g. an AND gate) without risk of partial pulses.
chunks.figure_note: Page 54 shows a waveform where an asynchronous signal A directly gates a clock-derived signal, producing a partial/glitched pulse at output X. Page 55 shows the fix: an edge-triggered D FF (clocked by the system clock, fed by the asynchronous signal) whose clean output then enables an AND gate synchronized to the clock's NGTs. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Detecting an Input Sequence with a Flip-Flop
chunks.summary: Flip-flops add a capability pure combinational logic lacks: detecting that inputs activated in a specific order/sequence, by using the FF's storage property; e.g. a clocked D FF can be arranged so its output activates only if input A goes HIGH before input B, with A leading B by at least the FF's setup time.
chunks.text: Combinational logic alone can only react to the CURRENT combination of input values — it has no memory of what order things happened in. Flip-flops add this missing capability because they can store the outcome of an earlier event and use it to condition a later one, enabling detection of a required INPUT SEQUENCE rather than just an input combination. Example: a clocked D flip-flop is arranged to respond only when input signal A goes HIGH, and this A-triggered value is then captured/used relative to a second signal B, so that the overall circuit's output activates only if A occurred in the correct order relative to B. For this sequence detection to work correctly and reliably, input A must transition HIGH before input B by at least an amount of time equal to the flip-flop's setup time (tS) — otherwise the FF might not have properly captured A's new state before it needs to be used, and the sequence could be missed or mis-detected.
chunks.figure_note: Page 56 shows the specific D-FF circuit wired to detect the A-before-B input sequence, with a waveform showing the required minimum A-to-B timing margin (>= setup time). Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Data Storage and Transfer: Registers, Synchronous vs Asynchronous, Parallel Transfer
chunks.summary: A group of flip-flops used for storage is called a register; data transfer between registers/FFs can be synchronous (occurring at a CLK edge) or asynchronous (controlled directly by PRE/CLR), and can move all bits at once (parallel transfer) or one bit at a time (serial transfer, covered in 5-17).
chunks.text:
Flip-flops are commonly grouped together for storage and transfer of multi-bit binary data. A group of FFs used this way is called a REGISTER. DATA TRANSFER occurs whenever data moves from one register/FF to another. There are two distinct mechanisms for triggering a transfer: Synchronous transfer takes place exactly at the active clock edge (PGT or NGT) of the destination FF's CLK input — this is the normal way data moves in a clocked system (e.g. using each FF's D or J/K synchronous inputs together with a shared clock line). Asynchronous transfer instead uses the destination FF's PRE and CLR (asynchronous) inputs directly, bypassing the clock entirely, to force each bit into its new value immediately.

A PARALLEL TRANSFER moves all the bits of a register simultaneously, in one clock event, by connecting each source bit to the corresponding destination FF and applying one common transfer pulse to all the destination CLK (or PRE/CLR) inputs at once — this is fast but requires as many wires as there are bits. (Serial transfer, which moves the bits of a register one at a time using far fewer interconnections, is covered separately in Section 5-17.)
chunks.figure_note: Page 58 shows several clocked FFs performing a synchronous transfer via their CLK inputs. Page 59 shows the same idea driven asynchronously via PRE/CLR inputs instead. Page 60 shows a register-to-register parallel transfer with all bit-lines connected simultaneously. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Serial Data Transfer and Shift Registers
chunks.summary: A shift register is a chain of flip-flops where, on every clock pulse, the stored bit in each FF moves to the next FF in the chain (serial transfer, one bit per clock). Worked example: two connected 3-bit shift registers fully transfer their contents (101) from register X to register Y in exactly 3 shift pulses.
chunks.text:
Transferring the bits of a register ONE AT A TIME (rather than all simultaneously) is called a serial transfer, and the circuit structure that performs it is a shift register: a group of flip-flops arranged so that, on each clock pulse, the binary value stored in each FF is shifted into the next FF in the chain. A four-bit shift register can be built from J-K flip-flops (each stage's Q/Q' outputs feeding the J/K inputs of the next stage) so that data entered at one end steps one position closer to the other end with each clock pulse; because the J and K inputs may be changing at nearly the same instant as the shared clock transition in this configuration, the FFs used in a shift register must have very small (ideally near-zero) hold-time requirements to shift reliably.

D flip-flops require fewer interconnections than J-K flip-flops for the same shift-register function (one data line per stage instead of two), so D-FF-based shift registers are common in practice. Worked example: two separate three-bit shift registers, X (holding 101, i.e. X2=1, X1=0, X0=1) and Y (initially 000), are connected so that X's contents serially transfer into Y. On each negative-going clock pulse, every FF in the chain takes on the value that was stored in the FF to its LEFT just prior to that pulse (this is how the shift propagates one position per pulse). Tracing it through: 
- After pulse 1: the bit from X2 shifts out toward Y2's chain position (and X's own internal bits also shift one place). 
- After pulse 2: further shifting occurs. 
- After pulse 3 (three total shift pulses for a 3-bit register): the COMPLETE transfer finishes — the value 1 originally in X2 ends up in Y2, the 0 originally in X1 ends up in Y1, and the 1 originally in X0 ends up in Y0. So Y now holds 101 (the value X originally held), while X has been emptied out to 000 (its original data is lost from X, having been shifted entirely into Y). In general, an N-bit shift register requires exactly N shift pulses to completely move its contents into a connected receiving register.

Data can equally well be arranged to shift right-to-left instead of left-to-right — neither direction is inherently better; the choice is dictated by the application. Compared with parallel transfer, serial transfer needs far fewer interconnecting wires between the sending and receiving registers (an advantage that grows with bit width) but is slower since it takes N clock pulses instead of 1; real systems often use a mix, exploiting parallel transfer's speed and serial transfer's economy/simplicity where each is advantageous.
chunks.figure_note: Page 62 shows a 4-bit J-K-flip-flop shift register schematic. Pages 64-69 show two connected 3-bit shift registers (X feeding Y) across successive clock pulses, tracing how the bit pattern 101 migrates from X into Y over 3 NGT clock pulses, ending with X=000 and Y=101. Not visually re-verified pixel-by-pixel since PDF rendering unavailable here, but the bit-transfer trace above follows directly and consistently from the slide captions on pages 64-69.

chunks.topic: Frequency Division and Binary Counting with Toggling J-K Flip-Flops
chunks.summary: Chaining J-K flip-flops in toggle mode (J=K=1) so each FF's output clocks the next produces a divide-by-2-per-stage frequency divider that simultaneously acts as a binary up-counter; three FFs give a MOD-8 counter (states 0-7), and each added FF doubles the modulus (MOD-16, etc.).
chunks.text:
Wiring J-K flip-flops in toggle mode (J tied HIGH, K tied HIGH) so that each FF's output feeds the CLK input of the next FF in the chain creates a frequency divider: each FF divides its own input clock frequency by exactly 2 (because a toggle FF flips once per input clock cycle, so its own output only completes one full cycle every TWO input cycles). Three such FFs chained together therefore produce an output frequency equal to 1/8 of the original input (clock) frequency; adding a fourth FF to the chain would make the output 1/16 of the original clock frequency.

The very same three-FF circuit doubles as a 3-bit binary counter: read together, the three FF outputs count in binary from 000(2) up through 111(2) — i.e. 0 through 7 in decimal — before rolling back over to 000 and repeating. This is called a MOD-8 (2^3) counter, and in general the number of distinct states a counter cycles through is called its modulus (MOD number). Adding one more toggling FF to the chain would create a MOD-16 (2^4) counter, counting 0 through 15 before rolling over; in general, N cascaded toggle FFs give a MOD-2^N counter.
chunks.figure_note: Pages 71-73 show three J-K flip-flops wired in toggle mode (J=K=1), each stage's Q output clocking the next stage's CLK input, forming a MOD-8 ripple counter/frequency divider; a timing/state diagram shows the outputs counting 000 through 111 before repeating. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Microcomputer Application of Registers
chunks.summary: Microprocessor units (MPUs) use external registers built from flip-flops to hold and transfer data for real-world control tasks such as solenoid/relay control, device positioning, and motor starting/speed control.
chunks.text: Microprocessor units (MPUs) rely heavily on registers (built from flip-flops) for data transfer and storage as part of their normal operation. Beyond internal use, MPUs frequently send data OUT to external registers connected to real-world devices, for purposes such as: controlling solenoids or relays, positioning mechanical devices, and starting motors or controlling their speed. In such an application, the MPU transfers a binary data word to an external register (a bank of flip-flops acting as a latch/buffer), and the stored bit pattern in that register then directly drives the external hardware (e.g. each bit turning on/off a particular relay or motor-control line) until the MPU updates it again.
chunks.figure_note: Page 75 shows a block diagram of a microprocessor transferring a binary data word over a bus into an external register, whose outputs then drive external control hardware. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Schmitt-Trigger Devices
chunks.summary: A Schmitt-trigger device is not technically a flip-flop but has a memory-like characteristic: it uses two separate switching thresholds (VT+ going up, VT- going down) so it converts a slow, noisy input into a fast, clean, oscillation-free output, 'remembering' the last threshold it crossed until the input reaches the opposite one.
chunks.text: A Schmitt-trigger device is not classified as a flip-flop, but exhibits a useful memory-like characteristic in certain situations. Its job is to accept a slowly-changing (or noisy) input signal and produce a clean output that transitions quickly and without oscillation. It achieves this via hysteresis: a Schmitt-trigger device has TWO distinct threshold voltages rather than one — a positive-going threshold VT+ and a negative-going threshold VT- (with VT+ > VT-). The device will not respond to (switch in response to) its input until the input actually exceeds whichever threshold is currently relevant. Because the two thresholds are separated (there is a gap between VT- and VT+), the device effectively 'remembers' which threshold it most recently crossed and will not switch back until the input swings all the way to the OPPOSITE threshold — this hysteresis gap is exactly what rejects noise: a small noisy wiggle near a single fixed threshold (as a standard, non-Schmitt inverter would use) can cause the standard inverter's output to chatter/oscillate, whereas the Schmitt-trigger device's output stays clean and switches only once per genuine slow transition.
chunks.figure_note: Page 77 shows a standard inverter's noisy/oscillating response to a slow, noisy input signal. Page 78 shows the same slow noisy input fed to a Schmitt-trigger device instead, producing a single, clean, fast output transition (no chatter). Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: One-Shot (Monostable Multivibrator)
chunks.summary: A one-shot (OS/monostable multivibrator) has one stable state; a trigger pulse drives it into a quasi-stable state for a fixed duration tp (set by external RC components) before it automatically returns to stable. Nonretriggerable one-shots ignore triggers while in the quasi-stable state; retriggerable one-shots restart their tp timer on each new trigger. The 74121 is a classic nonretriggerable IC example.
chunks.text:
Like a flip-flop, a one-shot (OS) has two outputs, Q and Q' (inverses of each other), but unlike a flip-flop it has only ONE stable state, which is why it is called a monostable multivibrator. A trigger event (typically a PGT) drives the OS from its stable state into a QUASI-STABLE state for a fixed time period tp, after which it automatically returns to the stable state on its own (no second trigger needed to return). The duration tp is usually set by an external resistor-capacitor (RC) time constant connected to dedicated timing pins, NOT by the duration of the trigger pulse itself — meaning OS output-pulse duration is always the same fixed tp, regardless of how long or short the triggering input pulse was; tp depends only on the external R, C values and the internal OS circuitry.

One-shots are prone to false triggering by noise (since they respond to any qualifying edge) and come in two behavioral flavors: Nonretriggerable devices, once triggered, ignore any further trigger pulses until they have fully returned to the stable state (finished their current tp interval) — additional trigger edges arriving during the quasi-stable period have NO effect. Retriggerable devices, by contrast, CAN be re-triggered while still in the quasi-stable state, and doing so restarts (extends) a fresh tp interval from that point — so a retriggerable OS fed with closely-spaced trigger pulses produces one long continuous output pulse instead of several separate ones.

The 74121 is a classic nonretriggerable one-shot IC. It contains internal gating logic that lets inputs A1, A2, and B all participate in triggering the OS (various logic combinations of A1/A2/B can each initiate a trigger); input B specifically is itself a Schmitt-trigger input, which allows it to tolerate slow input transition times while still reliably triggering the OS (leveraging the hysteresis behavior described in Section 5-20). External pins (labeled RINT for an internal timing resistor option, and REXT/CINT plus CEXT for external resistor/capacitor connections) let the designer set the desired output pulse duration tp by choosing appropriate R and C component values.
chunks.figure_note: Pages 81-83 show the OS symbol with waveforms illustrating nonretriggerable operation: trigger edges at points a,b,c,e each produce a full tp pulse, while edges at points d,f (arriving during an already-active quasi-stable period) have no effect. Page 84 compares nonretriggerable vs retriggerable OS responses for tp=2ms side by side; page 85 shows a retriggerable OS restarting its tp interval on each new trigger. Page 86 shows the 74121 IC pinout/internal-gate diagram with A1, A2, B inputs and RINT/REXT-CINT/CEXT timing pins. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Clock Generator Circuits (Astable Multivibrators, 555 Timer, Crystal Oscillators)
chunks.summary: An astable (free-running) multivibrator has no stable state and continuously switches between two unstable states, making it useful for generating clock signals; implementations include a Schmitt-trigger inverter oscillator, the 555 timer IC (built around two comparators and an S-R latch), and crystal-controlled oscillators for high-stability applications like microprocessor systems.
chunks.text:
An astable (free-running) multivibrator is a third fundamental multivibrator type (alongside the bistable flip-flop and the monostable one-shot) that has NO stable state at all — it continuously and automatically switches back and forth between two unstable states on its own, with no external trigger needed. This self-sustaining oscillation makes astable circuits the standard way to generate clock signals for synchronous digital systems.

One simple implementation is a Schmitt-trigger oscillator built from a single 7414 Schmitt-trigger INVERTER (a 7413 Schmitt-trigger NAND gate can be substituted) wired with an external RC feedback network: the capacitor repeatedly charges/discharges between the inverter's two hysteresis thresholds, causing the output to continuously oscillate at a frequency set by the R and C values.

The 555 timer IC is a widely-used, TTL-compatible device that can be configured for several different modes, including as an astable multivibrator producing a repetitive rectangular output waveform whose HIGH-time and LOW-time durations are independently set by external R and C component values. Internally, the heart of the 555 timer consists of two voltage comparators feeding an internal S-R latch: each comparator outputs HIGH whenever the voltage on its (+) input exceeds the voltage on its (-) input, and the resulting comparator outputs set/reset the internal latch to produce the oscillating output.

For applications demanding a very stable, accurate clock frequency — such as microprocessor and microcomputer systems where precise timing intervals are essential — a crystal-controlled oscillator is used instead of an RC-based astable circuit, since a quartz crystal's mechanical resonance provides far better frequency stability (over time, temperature, and supply-voltage variation) than an RC time constant can.
chunks.figure_note: Page 88 shows a 7414 Schmitt-trigger-inverter RC oscillator circuit. Page 90 shows the 555 timer IC wired as an astable multivibrator (with its external R1, R2, C timing network). Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here; the internal 555 description (two comparators + S-R latch) is transcribed directly from the slide text.

chunks.topic: Troubleshooting Flip-Flop Circuits: Noise Sensitivity and Clock Skew
chunks.summary: FFs are subject to the same faults as combinational logic, plus timing-specific faults not seen in pure combinational circuits: unconnected/floating inputs are especially vulnerable to noise-induced glitches that FFs (unlike gates) will latch and hold permanently; clock skew (the same clock signal arriving at different FFs at different times, often due to extra gating in the clock path) can cause intermittent, hard-to-reproduce faults.
chunks.text:
Flip-flops are subject to the same categories of internal/external faults described for combinational logic in Chapter 4, but additionally have TIMING-related faults and symptoms that pure combinational circuits do not exhibit. Unconnected or floating FF inputs are especially susceptible to spurious voltage fluctuations (noise): given sufficient noise amplitude and duration, ANY logic circuit's output may momentarily change state in response to noise, but the behavior differs critically between combinational gates and flip-flops — a combinational gate's output will return to its correct value automatically once the noise subsides, whereas a flip-flop's output will REMAIN in the new (incorrect) state indefinitely, because of the flip-flop's memory characteristic (it has no way to know the change was spurious). This makes floating/noisy FF inputs a much more serious and persistent fault than the equivalent situation in combinational logic.

Clock skew occurs when the same nominal clock signal arrives at different flip-flops in a synchronous system at slightly different times (rather than truly simultaneously) — often introduced by extra gating circuitry inserted somewhere in the clock distribution path (e.g. an AND/OR gate used to enable/disable the clock for one group of FFs but not another), which adds propagation delay to that branch of the clock tree relative to others. Because skew-induced faults depend on the exact relative timing between FFs, they may appear only intermittently under certain conditions, or may disappear entirely when probed with test equipment (since adding a scope probe can itself alter the circuit's loading/timing) — making clock skew one of the more difficult classes of digital fault to diagnose.
chunks.figure_note: Pages 94-95 show example circuits where extra gating logic placed in the clock path to different FFs introduces differing propagation delays, causing clock skew between those FFs. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Sequential Circuits in PLDs: Schematic Entry and HDL (Feedback and Latching)
chunks.summary: PLD development tools (e.g. Quartus II) let designers build and simulate sequential circuits via schematic capture using megafunction libraries before programming real hardware; in HDL, sequential/latching behavior is created by feeding an output signal back to its own input logic, which must be designed carefully to avoid unwanted oscillation.
chunks.text:
Modern PLD development software (the slides reference Altera's Quartus II) lets designers describe sequential circuits using schematic diagrams, drawing on a megafunction library of pre-built high-level modules (counters, registers, etc.) rather than building every flip-flop from individual gates. The built-in simulator allows the sequential circuit's behavior to be verified in software before the design is actually programmed into a physical PLD, catching logical/timing errors early and cheaply.

When describing sequential circuits directly in an HDL (rather than via schematic capture), most PLD architectures allow a port/signal to feed its own output value back into its input-side logic — this output-with-feedback is exactly what's needed to implement latching (memory) behavior in HDL, mirroring how a NAND/NOR latch's gate outputs feed back into the cross-coupled inputs at the gate level. For example, the behavioral HDL description of an S-R latch directly encodes this feedback relationship rather than instantiating discrete NAND/NOR gates.

A key hazard of this feedback approach: whenever a circuit's output value is fed back into its own input logic, a change in output state CAN, in principle, change the input conditions, which changes the output state again, which feeds back again, and so on — creating unwanted continuous oscillation if the feedback loop isn't controlled correctly. It is therefore very important, when writing such HDL descriptions, to verify that NO combination of inputs and outputs can trigger this kind of runaway/undesirable self-oscillation — i.e., the design must guarantee that the feedback loop always settles into one of the intended stable states for every reachable input/output combination.
chunks.figure_note: Page 98 shows an HDL behavioral-description diagram/logic for an S-R latch built via output feedback rather than discrete gates. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.
